In mathematics, especially [[algebraic geometry]], the '''decomposition theorem of Beilinson, Bernstein, Deligne and Gabber''' or '''BBDG decomposition''' theorem is a set of results concerning the cohomology of [[algebraic variety|algebraic varieties]]. It was originally conjectured by Gelfand and MacPherson.<ref>Conjecture 2.10. of Sergei Gelfand & Robert MacPherson, Verma modules and Schubert cells: A dictionary.</ref>

==Statement==

===Decomposition for smooth proper maps===
The first case of the decomposition theorem arises via the [[hard Lefschetz theorem]] which gives isomorphisms, for a smooth [[proper map]] <math>f: X \to Y</math> of relative dimension ''d'' between two projective varieties<ref>{{citation|last=Deligne|first=Pierre|title=Théoreme de Lefschetz et critères de dégénérescence de suites spectrales|journal=Publ. Math. Inst. Hautes Études Sci.|volume=35|pages=107–126|year=1968|doi=10.1007/BF02698925|zbl=0159.22501|s2cid=121086388|url=https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1968__35__107_0/|hdl=2013/ULB-DIPOT:oai:dipot.ulb.ac.be:2013/215173|hdl-access=free}}</ref>
:<math>- \cup \eta^i : R^{d-i}f_* (\mathbb Q) \stackrel \cong \to R^{d+i} f_*(\mathbb Q).</math>
Here <math>\eta</math> is the [[fundamental class]] of a [[hyperplane section]], <math>f_*</math> is the [[direct image]] (pushforward) and <math>R^n f_*</math> is the ''n''-th [[derived functor]] of the direct image. This derived functor measures the ''n''-th cohomologies of <math>f^{-1}(U)</math>, for <math>U \subset Y</math>.
In fact, the particular case when ''Y'' is a point, amounts to the isomorphism
:<math>- \cup \eta^i : H^{d-i} (X, \mathbb Q) \stackrel \cong \to H^{d+i} (X, \mathbb Q).</math>

This hard Lefschetz isomorphism induces canonical isomorphisms
:<math>Rf_* (\mathbb Q) \stackrel \cong \to \bigoplus_{i=-d}^{d} R^{d+i} f_*(\mathbb Q)[-d-i].</math>
Moreover, the sheaves <math>R^{d+i} f_* \mathbb Q</math> appearing in this decomposition are [[local system]]s, i.e., locally free sheaves of '''Q'''-vector spaces, which are moreover semisimple, i.e., a direct sum of local systems without nontrivial local subsystems.

===Decomposition for proper maps===
The decomposition theorem generalizes this fact to the case of a proper, but not necessarily smooth map <math>f: X \to Y</math> between varieties. In a nutshell, the results above remain true when the notion of local systems is replaced by [[perverse sheaf|perverse sheaves]].

The hard Lefschetz theorem above takes the following form:<ref name="cohomology decomposition">{{harvnb|Beilinson|Bernstein|Deligne|1982|loc=Théorème 6.2.10.}}. NB: To be precise, the reference is for the decomposition.</ref><ref>{{harvnb|MacPherson|1990|loc=Theorem 1.12.}} NB: To be precise, the reference is for the decomposition.</ref> there is an isomorphism in the [[derived category]] of sheaves on ''Y'':
:<math>{}^p H^{-i} (Rf_* \mathbb Q) \cong  {}^p H^{+i} (Rf_* \mathbb Q),</math>
where <math>Rf_*</math> is the total derived functor of <math>f_*</math> and <math>{}^p H^i</math> is the ''i''-th truncation with respect to the ''perverse'' [[t-structure]].

Moreover, there is an isomorphism
:<math>Rf_* IC_X^\bullet \cong \bigoplus_i {}^p H^i (Rf_* IC_X^\bullet)[-i].</math>
where the summands are semi-simple perverse-sheaves, meaning they are direct sums of push-forwards of intersection cohomology sheaves.<ref>{{harvnb|Beilinson|Bernstein|Deligne|1982|loc=Théorème 6.2.5.}}</ref>

If ''X'' is not smooth, then the above results remain true when <math>\mathbb Q[\dim X]</math> is replaced by the [[intersection cohomology]] complex <math>IC</math>.<ref name="cohomology decomposition" />

==Proofs==
The decomposition theorem was first proved by Beilinson, Bernstein, Deligne and Gabber.<ref>{{cite journal
| last1 = Beilinson
| first1 = Alexander A.
| author-link = Alexander Beilinson
| authorlink2 = Joseph Bernstein
| first2=Joseph |last2=Bernstein
| authorlink3=Pierre Deligne
| first3=Pierre |last3=Deligne
| year = 1982
| title = Faisceaux pervers
| journal = Astérisque
| volume = 100
| publisher = Société Mathématique de France, Paris
| language = French
}}
</ref> Their proof is based on the usage of weights on l-adic sheaves in positive characteristic. A different proof using [[mixed Hodge module]]s was given by Saito. A more geometric proof, based on the notion of '''semismall maps''' was given by de Cataldo and Migliorini.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=de Cataldo|first1=Mark Andrea|author1-link=Mark de Cataldo|last2=Migliorini|first2=Luca|title=The Hodge theory of algebraic maps|journal=Annales Scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure|volume=38|issue=5|pages=693–750|year=2005|doi = 10.1016/j.ansens.2005.07.001|url=https://www.numdam.org/item?id=ASENS_2005_4_38_5_693_0|arxiv=math/0306030|bibcode=2003math......6030D|s2cid=54046571}}</ref>

For semismall maps, the decomposition theorem also applies to [[Chow motive]]s.<ref>{{citation|author1-link=Mark de Cataldo
|last1=de Cataldo|first1=Mark Andrea|last2=Migliorini|first2=Luca|title=The Chow motive of semismall resolutions|journal=Math. Res. Lett.|volume=11|year=2004|issue=2–3|pages=151–170|mr=2067464|doi=10.4310/MRL.2004.v11.n2.a2|arxiv=math/0204067|s2cid=53323330}}</ref>

== Applications of the theorem ==
=== Cohomology of a Rational Lefschetz Pencil ===
Consider a rational morphism <math>f:X \rightarrow \mathbb{P}^1</math> from a smooth quasi-projective variety given by <math>[f_1(x):f_2(x)]</math>. If we set the vanishing locus of <math>f_1,f_2</math> as <math>Y</math> then there is an induced morphism <math>\tilde{X} = Bl_Y(X) \to \mathbb{P}^1</math>. We can compute the cohomology of <math>X</math> from the intersection cohomology of <math>Bl_Y(X)</math> and subtracting off the cohomology from the blowup along <math>Y</math>. This can be done using the perverse [[spectral sequence]]
:<math> E_2^{l,m} = H^l(\mathbb{P}^1; {}^\mathfrak{p}\mathcal{H}^m(IC_{\tilde{X}}^\bullet(\mathbb{Q})) \Rightarrow IH^{l + m}(\tilde{X};\mathbb{Q}) \cong H^{l+m}(X;\mathbb{Q})</math>

=== Local invariant cycle theorem ===
{{main|local invariant cycle theorem}}
Let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be a [[proper morphism]] between complex algebraic varieties such that <math>X</math> is smooth. Also, let <math>y_0</math> be a regular value of <math>f</math> that is in an open ball ''B'' centered at <math>y</math>. Then the restriction map
:<math>\operatorname{H}^*(f^{-1}(y), \mathbb{Q}) = \operatorname{H}^*(f^{-1}(B), \mathbb{Q}) \to \operatorname{H}^*(f^{-1}(y_0), \mathbb{Q})^{\pi_{1, \textrm{loc}}}</math>
is surjective, where <math>\pi_{1, \textrm{loc}}</math> is the fundamental group of the intersection of <math>B</math> with the set of regular values of ''f''.<ref>{{harvnb|de Cataldo|2015|loc=Theorem 1.4.1.}}</ref>
